clue.text: Cry hard for one born in error

parts.note: a boo-boo is a silly mistake
b. = born, as in biographies; one of the two Bs is taken out
H = hard, as on pencils; it goes in where the B was

explanation.surface: Someone weeping bitterly over a baby born by mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The pencil grade H for hard replaces the second B of BOOBOO. 'Born in error' reads as a whole phrase about a baby, but it splits into two separate pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Boo-hoo is the noise of loud crying, used as a verb for weeping noisily.

clue.text: Reader separated from a drug addict

parts.note: a peruser is someone who reads something through
per = a, as in 'ten pounds a head'; this is removed

explanation.surface: A reader cut off from someone hooked on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The tiny word 'a' does the heavy lifting: it means PER, as in 'twice a day', and PERUSER without PER leaves USER.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is the everyday slang term for someone who takes illegal drugs.

clue.text: Clubs welcome punishment that player might be dealt

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase for a bridge hand, standing for the noun

parts.note: C = clubs, the card suit
hi is an informal greeting
a caning was an old school punishment

explanation.surface: A card player being punished for welcoming clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs, player and dealt all point at cards, but only in bridge does chicane mean a hand with no trumps; most solvers know it as a tight bend on a racing circuit.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge a chicane is a hand dealt to a player containing no trumps.

clue.text: Camels wandering about every second minute

indicators.note: the letters of CAMELS stray from their order
the rearranged camels go around the other letters

parts.note: CAMELS rearranged, to be split around ALL + S
all = every
s = second, the unit of time

explanation.surface: Camels roaming around once every other minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second minute' looks like a single phrase about timing, but it splits into ALL, S and the definition. Minute here is pronounced my-NEWT, meaning tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Something small-scale is tiny in extent, which is what minute means.

clue.text: Analyses aircraft series, each one of these perhaps more than one?

definitions.text: Analyses aircraft series, each one of these perhaps more than one?

parts.note: reads as a phrase about studying aircraft production; really a list of three sample nouns

parts.words: each one of these perhaps more than one?
parts.note: each listed word can name more than one thing, which is the grammatical form wanted

explanation.surface: A trade magazine studying series of aircraft, each type possibly built in more than one.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three words read as a sentence about aviation, but they are really just a list: analyses, aircraft and series are each plural nouns, and 'perhaps' warns that aircraft and series can also be singular.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural word refers to more than one thing, and each of the three listed nouns is one.

clue.text: "M" is inserted into Parisian street name retrospectively

indicators.note: looking backwards, so the whole string is read in reverse

parts.note: rue is French for street
used as it stands
nom is French for name; 'Parisian' covers it too

explanation.surface: A letter M being slotted into a Paris street name after the fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'M' in quotes is the definition: it is the French abbreviation for Monsieur, as in M. Poirot. 'Parisian' makes both RUE and NOM French.
explanation.definitionFit: M. is the standard written abbreviation of the French title Monsieur.

clue.text: Chuck the actor small golf club to hold Resistance back

indicators.note: to hold is to keep inside
the finished string is read backwards

parts.note: s = small, as on clothing labels
an iron is a type of golf club
R = resistance in physics

explanation.surface: Telling an actor to throw a small golf club while holding back the Resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' looks like a verb meaning throw, but it is the actor's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Chuck Norris is the American martial-arts film actor.

clue.text: Perhaps Queen Victoria admits "you can't trust me with very outstanding artworks"

parts.note: Regina Imperatrix, Victoria's title as queen and empress; 'perhaps' because other queens qualify
someone who says I LIE is not to be trusted
v = very

explanation.surface: Queen Victoria confessing she cannot be trusted with very fine paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: RI appears on Victorian coins after VICTORIA D G BRITT REG, standing for Regina Imperatrix. 'Outstanding' means literally standing out from the surface, not excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Rilievi is the plural of rilievo, a relief sculpture whose figures stand out from the background.

clue.text: Hotel chain features in The Morning Show

parts.note: Hilton is an international hotel chain
a.m. = morning

explanation.surface: A hotel chain appearing on a breakfast television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Morning Show' looks like a TV title, but the show is the definition on its own. Lewis Hamilton is one of the grid's British Formula One champions.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamilton is the hit Broadway hip-hop musical about Alexander Hamilton.

clue.text: Angry man of God blockades useless house

indicators.note: read literally as use-less: the word house less its letters USE

parts.note: a cleric is a clergyman
HOUSE without USE leaves HO

explanation.surface: A furious priest besieging a house that serves no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Useless' is read literally, as HOUSE less USE, rather than as worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Choleric describes someone bad-tempered and easily angered.

clue.text: They sing high notes, closing intros from Rihanna & Kylie

indicators.note: the notes close around the two initials

parts.note: la is a note of the sol-fa scale, so two are LAS

indicators.note: only the first letter of each name is used

parts.note: the first letters of each singer's name

explanation.surface: Pop singers hitting high notes as the introductions from two stars bring a show to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High notes' looks like one phrase, but 'high' ends the definition and 'notes' starts the wordplay; 'closing' means enclosing, not ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Skylarks famously sing while climbing high into the sky.

clue.text: The greatest possible car competition is out of line

parts.note: a rally is a motoring competition
RY = railway, a line; removed

explanation.surface: A top motor race being ruled out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: Line for railway is a crossword convention; here its two letters come from opposite ends of the competition.
explanation.definitionFit: All, as in 'with all speed', means the greatest possible amount.

clue.text: Dickens veto curbs the writer's self-esteem in retirement

parts.note: a ban = a veto

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so MY EGO is reversed

parts.note: the writer's = MY, self-esteem = EGO

explanation.surface: A ban on Charles Dickens limiting an author's pride once he has retired.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens is not the novelist: 'the dickens' is an old euphemism for the devil, as in 'what the dickens?'
explanation.definitionFit: The dickens is a mild name for the devil, and the bogeyman is a similar evil spirit.

clue.text: Head of Maths at university helping development

indicators.note: the first letter of Maths

parts.note: first letter of Maths
used as it stands
U = university
a helping or ration is a portion of food

explanation.surface: A head of maths department at a university helping with a project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like a verb but is the noun, a serving of food.
explanation.definitionFit: Maturation is the process of growing and developing to maturity.

clue.text: Keeper of the shop vault on report

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is spoken

parts.note: a cellar is an underground vault

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's underground strongroom being mentioned in a report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vault' suggests jumping; here it is a noun meaning an underground store.
explanation.definitionFit: A seller keeps a shop and sells its goods.

clue.text: Performer moving from #3 to #9 in chart is Tems

indicators.note: take letters three to nine of the following words

parts.note: count along the letters of these three words and take numbers three to nine

explanation.surface: The singer Tems climbing from third to ninth in the pop charts.
explanation.walkthrough: Tems is a Nigerian singer, so the surface is a chart report; moving up from number three to nine would be a fall, a joke the numbers hide.
explanation.definitionFit: An artiste is a professional entertainer such as a singer or dancer.

clue.text: I drive horses nearly mad on heading across motorway

parts.note: re = on the subject of

indicators.note: INSANE loses its last letter

parts.note: INSANE without its final E
M = motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A coachman admitting he drives horses almost to madness on the way over a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is written in the first person: the answer is saying 'I drive horses'.
explanation.definitionFit: A reinsman is a skilled driver of horses, especially in harness racing.

clue.text: Ukraine is the reverse of corrupt in counsel

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; with 'is' it describes Ukraine

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word read backwards

parts.note: to warn = to counsel or advise
to rot is to decay or corrupt

explanation.surface: A claim that Ukraine is the opposite of corrupt in its advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a political statement about corruption, but 'Ukraine is' defines by example, so it is simply a description of the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukraine, invaded by Russia, is torn apart by war.

clue.text: Try the Guinness? Hotel's out!

parts.note: Guinness is a stout, a dark beer
H = hotel in the NATO alphabet; removed

explanation.surface: An offer of a Guinness, followed by the news that the hotel has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'out' in the clue also turns up in the answer: removing H from THE STOUT gives TESTOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to test something out is to try it in practice before relying on it.

clue.text: Design event's launch is held in the City

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London; it holds T
a thing is an event, as in 'a big thing'; its first letter T goes into EC
the rest of THING follows

explanation.surface: A design show's opening being staged in the financial district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the launch of the event moves, into the City's postcode, while the rest of the word stays put. The City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a design or picture printed from an etched plate.

clue.text: Unusual grub is a feature of California

indicators.note: the letters appear in an unusual order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: Strange food being a speciality of California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' is food, pointing at Californian cuisine; the definition is the geography.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Sur is a rugged stretch of the central California coast.

clue.text: Look to fine breaks close to Rimini

indicators.note: to break something is to split it open
the last letter of Rimini

parts.note: to push a door to is to shut it
f = fine, as on pencils
last letter of Rimini

explanation.surface: A glance at a nice break on the Italian coast near Rimini.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is not a link but the adverb meaning closed, as in 'pull the door to'. Shufti is British slang, from Arabic, for a quick look.
explanation.definitionFit: A shufti is British slang for a quick look.

clue.text: Ofsted is seething about ring-fencing NE region

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters read backwards
the words fence the answer in, hiding it

parts.note: ofst(ED IS SEET)hing

explanation.surface: School inspectors fuming over protected funding in the north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is the English schools inspectorate, and ring-fencing is protecting a budget, so the surface is education politics. Teesside is the area around the River Tees in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Teesside is the industrial region around the lower River Tees in north-east England.

clue.text: Insurgent not initially required to procure fine butcher's hooks

indicators.note: rising up, so in this down clue the letters read upwards
ASKED loses its first letter

parts.note: ASKED without its first letter
OK = fine

explanation.surface: A rebel butcher obtaining decent meat hooks without being asked first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's hook' is Cockney rhyming slang for look, and dekko is British slang for a look, so both halves are slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Dekkos are looks, and butcher's hooks are looks in rhyming slang.

clue.text: Section of circular circuit

indicators.note: of means coming from, so the answer is taken out of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Part of a round racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular circuit' reads as a racing track, but the words only supply letters; the answer spans the join between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometric sense: an arc is a section of a curve, such as part of a circle's circumference.

clue.text: Switch pipe down, then turn it off and on

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

indicators.note: take a letter, skip a letter, alternately

parts.note: t(U)r(N)i(T): every second letter

explanation.surface: Instructions for a noisy switch: silence it, then turn it off and on again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn it off and on' is the classic tech-support fix, but here 'off and on' picks letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To shunt a train is to switch it onto another track.

clue.text: With various pikes sees off unfriendly superior

indicators.note: C's (two letter Cs) are sent off from the words

parts.note: CHILL = unfriendly, losing its C
COCKY = superior or self-important, losing its C

explanation.surface: A cold, snooty person driving off enemies with an assortment of spears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pikes' suggests weapons or fish, but a pike is a peak in the Lake District, such as Scafell Pike. 'Sees' is the plural of the letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: Hillocky ground is full of small hills, or pikes.

clue.text: Division heading north along border of Chile and Bolivia?

indicators.note: north is up the page, so in a down clue the letters read upwards
a border is where two places meet, so take the letters where Chile's end touches the start of Bolivia

parts.note: the last letter of Chile, its edge next to Bolivia
first letters: the opening three letters of Bolivia, its edge next to Chile

explanation.surface: A territory running north along the Chile–Bolivia frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The '?' flags that the border is between the printed words, not the countries; 'and' just joins the two names and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobe is a rounded division of an organ such as the brain or lung.

clue.text: Being received by dynasty with gold bar I may

indicators.note: bar means except, so WITH is taken without its I

parts.note: the Han dynasty ruled China
WITH without I
or = gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone being welcomed into a royal house with a gold ingot, asking permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I may' reads as asking permission, hiding the definition: May is another name for hawthorn, whose blossom appears in May. The I belongs to 'bar I'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawthorn is also called may, after the month it flowers.

clue.text: Trump's backside in contact with switch

parts.note: butt is American slang for backside
on = touching, in contact with

explanation.surface: A jab at Donald Trump's rear end touching a switch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Trump's' gives an American flavour, so BUTT is the US word for bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A button is a switch you press to turn something on or off.
